The Airport Spur Air Quality Report did not show a full understanding of what constitutes degradation. The degradation of air quality which a receptor suffers is the increase in carbon monoxide to which he or she is exposed as a result of completion of the proposed source of air pollution. When a receptor will be exposed to a certain amount of carbon monoxide emitted by nearby traffic even if the facility is not built, then the degradation increment must be determined by subtracting the "no build" concentration from the "build" concentration. The enclosed flow diagram illustrating the procedure for reviewing a notice of intent has been revised to make this clearer.
The purpose of determining whether the one-hour carbon monoxide concentration is greater than 3 1/3 parts per million, as called for in the old flow diagram, was also misunderstood (page 121). This was only meant to simplify the screening procedure by eliminating the calculation of the eight-hour carbon monoxide maximum for small projects proposed for areas where the background carbon monoxide concentration is so low that there is no danger that the project will cause a violation of the national ambient air quality standard. A one-hour maximum of less than 3 1/3 parts per million is sufficiently low to protect the eight-hour increment of two parts per million because the average traffic volume during the eight-hour peak cannot be more than the peak hour volume. If the two are equal, applying the EPA meteorological persistence factor of .6 to a one-hour maximum of 3 1/3 parts per million gives an eight-hour maximum of two parts per million.
Since for any project in an urban area (where background cannot be assumed to be low) the eight-hour maximum must be calculated, even if the increment caused by a facility is less than two parts per million, to determine if total receptor exposure is more than 75% of the eight-hour standard, the revised flow sheet bypasses the 3 1/3 parts per million box in such cases. Comparison of the one-hour maximum to 3 1/3 parts per million will not be needed for any highway project in the Milwaukee area.
Information giving the approximate location of the different receptors which was included in earlier versions of the air quality report was omitted from the October version, except for receptor number five. The air quality report should include sufficient information to permit the microscale calculations to be repeated for all receptor sites analyzed. This could be given as a table of distances from each receptor to the relevant lanes of traffic, or it could be in the form of a scale drawing or aerial photograph on which approximate distance measurements could be made.
The air quality report did not state whether the relocated Grange Avenue or air cargo area road intersections with Howell Avenue were signalized or non-signalized. The statement is made on page 108 that the air quality calculations were based on free-flow traffic conditions. Did this apply to receptor number six near Howell Avenue as well as those at the other end of the Spur? When the EPA screening technique is applied to traffic near an intersection, the curves used are different from those which apply to free-flowing traffic uninfluenced by an intersection.
